title: Balfour: objective, plate caption, serial section, and microtome crosswalk
research_problem: Cambridge preserves Balfour's embryological serial sections, microscope objectives and departmental microtome apparatus. The unusually high-value route is not merely that these things coexist: the Whipple Museum states that acquisition dates of some objectives can be traced through mentions in captions to plates in Balfour's papers.

objective_archive.repository: Whipple Museum of the History of Science
objective_archive.provenance: On loan from the University of Cambridge Department of Zoology; belonged to Francis Maitland Balfour.
objective_archive.critical_museum_note: The museum records that Balfour kept in contact with Zeiss and acquired new lenses, and that dates of acquisition of different lenses can to some extent be traced from their mention in captions to plates in Balfour's papers. It warns that some 1882 engravings are probably commemorative and should not be read as acquisition dates.
objective_archive.research_value: Plate captions can potentially act as dated use records for specific objective designations/performances, turning publication paratext into an instrument-acquisition source.

microtome_archive.provenance: Donated by Cambridge Department of Zoology in 2021
microtome_archive.contemporary_text_bridge: The Whipple description identifies this type as the microtome described in Foster and Balfour, Elements of Embryology, as the one 'we are most accustomed to'.
microtome_archive.technical_note: This sliding model is pre-1880 and was not automatic/ribbon-producing.
microtome_archive.guard: Departmental provenance and textual familiarity do not prove that accession 6766 cut a particular surviving Balfour series.

later_apparatus_guard.significance: It belongs to the immediate post-Balfour Cambridge problem of producing regular ribbons of sections and was developed after Caldwell's suggestion.
later_apparatus_guard.guard: Do not back-project the automatic machine onto Balfour's earlier serial sections. It is a successor solution to a production problem, not evidence for Balfour's own slide manufacture.

crosswalk_method: Build a list of every objective designation/number visible on the surviving Balfour optics.
Search Balfour's papers, books and plate captions for Zeiss/Gundlach objective designations, focal lengths, apertures, immersion language and magnification notes.
Record the earliest secure printed mention for each objective as a terminus ante quem for use/acquisition, without using 1882 commemorative engraving as dating proof.
For each plate/figure mention, identify the anatomical preparation or embryological stage represented.
Then query Cambridge Museum of Zoology surviving Balfour serial sections for the same taxon/stage/series and original catalogue/notebook references.
Only assign a surviving objective to a surviving section if a documentary source explicitly joins them; otherwise maintain a bounded apparatus pool.
article_payoff: This case can make instrument use historically specific without turning into instrument biography. A lens becomes visible through a plate caption; a serial section becomes visible through a publication figure; the microtome structures the production of the series. The research object is the crosswalk among apparatus, preparation and printed image.
first_action: Before requesting broad Cambridge archival digitisation, extract all objective references from Balfour plate captions. The museum itself identifies this as the route capable of dating the lens set.
